Q: What is the difference between SynchronizationContext.Send and SynchronizationContext.Post? A:

but I can't explain why it uses SynchronizationContext.Send from the thread-pool and Synchronization.Post from the Func passed into the method that does the heavy lifting

1). using callback, as your delegate, from UI-thread (that you capture in your _ExecuteCommand), you can get deadlock if waiting it synchronously (if use Send), synchronous waiting is blocking, therefore Post should be used there.

Send is synchronous (blocking), while Post is asynchronous (non-blocking).

In Send example code - you can get deadlock:

context.Send(state => {
    // This runs on the UI thread
    myLabel.Text = "Updated from background";
}, null);   // deadlock is possible

2). but using thread of ThreadPool you can Send your message about either completion or exception asynchronously back to your captured SynchronizationContext (either UI or any other), and you're not going to wait for anything in sending thread, as it have finished its work already

3). besides, for WinForms and WPF, Post may not invoke delegate directly (therefore you capture SynchronizationContext to do Action on it), Send can invoke delegate directly, if called from UI thread.

p.s. for WPF you can use DispatcherSynchronizationContext

Q: Why isn't Staged Migration working for my App? A:

I've spent quite some time testing how the staged migration works, and I think I figured out most of the nuances with NSLightweightMigrationStage.

I want to share my finding in as many places as possible so that other troubled developers would be able to find this info and avoid the struggle 😇

The experimental project:

The model

  • V1 initial

  • V2 added Required String name

  • V3 added Required UUID id

  • V4 added Optional String bs

  • V5 added Optional Int attr5. Default: 0

  • V6 added Optional Int attr6. Changed attr5 default to 2

  • V7 added Optional String attr7. Chanded attr5 default to 4.

  • V8 added Required Int count. Default: 0.

  • V9 deleted attr7.

  • V10 deleted attr6

Custom Mappings

I've also included Model Mapping files with some custom policies:

  • V1 => V2: Fills name field from the custom policy's function.

  • V2 => V3: Fills id with new generated UUIDs from custom policy's function.

  • V4 => V5: Fills attr5 with a random number from 1 to 10 through the custom policy.

  • V7 => V8: Fills count with a random number from 1 to 10 through the custom policy.

And here's what I found

  1. NSLightweightMigrationStage allows to combine migration of several model versions into a single step. For V3-V7 models one lightweight stage can perform migration from any V3-V6 to V7. Which can be very useful when the span of versions that can be lightweight-migrated becomes longer. This is probably the biggest reason to not give up on it 🙂

  2. Having one NSLightweightMigrationStage with multiple versionChecksums seems to be the same as having one NSLightweightMigrationStage per versionChecksum. The migration process still infers mapping from the earliest version to the latest in the list.

The:


// ...

NSLightweightMigrationStage([V4, V5, V6]),

// ...

Does the same as:


// ...

NSLightweightMigrationStage([V4]),

NSLightweightMigrationStage([V5]),

NSLightweightMigrationStage([V6]),

// ...

#1 and #2 Tested by setting different Default Value of attr5 for each model version and inspecting sqlite database after migration to see the final value in the ZATTR5 column. It always had Default Value from the latest version to which the migration was performed (e.g. in V3 => V6, the value would be 2, while in V3 => V7 the value would be 4). Contrary, when migrating by manually incrementing versions, attr5 would be set to 0 after V4=>V5 and would remain 0 for all subsequent migrations.

  1. Order of the versionChecksums in NSLightweightMigrationStage.init seems to have no impact on the outcome.

The:


NSLightweightMigrationStage([V4, V5, V6])

Does the same as:


NSLightweightMigrationStage([V5, V6, V4])

#3 Tested by mixing V4, V5 and V6 versions in the same stage and observing the same results.

  1. NSLightweightMigrationStage does not use any custom Model Mapping files that automatic migration usually picks up.

#4 Tested by providing Model Mapping file with a custom policy for V4 to V5, while performing NSLightweightMigrationStage([V4, V5, V6]). Policy did not get called and didn't generate random numbers for attr5.

  1. When NSLightweightMigrationStage appears between NSCustomMigrationStages, it should only include intermediate "checkpoints":

// ...

NSCustomMigrationStage(migratingFrom: V2, to: V3),

NSLightweightMigrationStage([V4, V5, V6]), // intermediates only

NSCustomMigrationStage(migratingFrom: V7, to: V8)

// ...

Attempting to provide either V3 or V7 in lightweight stage would throw the exception with duplicated checksums. The end goal here is to let manager know about all existing versions of the model that take part in migration process.

#5 Tested by ensuring that Default Value for attr5 from V6 is set in the final version, and custom mapping is performed when going from V7 to V8.

  1. When there are no intermediate versions between NSCustomMigrationStages, a NSLightweightMigrationStage must still be included with no versions (e.g. [] - empty array). Omitting it would cause migration to ignore the next NSCustomMigrationStage:

// ...

NSCustomMigrationStage(migratingFrom: V2, to: V3),

NSLightweightMigrationStage([]), // must be here

NSCustomMigrationStage(migratingFrom: V4, to: V5)

// ...

#6 Tested by removing NSLightweightMigrationStage([]) and observing that V4 to V5 custom migration policy wasn't run. Migration failed because manager had no info how to get from V3 to V4, and the next custom stage tried to open the store assuming it is V4 while it's still V3.

  1. When NSLightweightMigrationStage appears at the beginning or the end of the list (e.g. for the first and latest model versions), it should include corresponding model version. The reason is that all model versions that take part in migration process should be registered/claimed by on of the stages of migration:

// ...

NSCustomMigrationStage(migratingFrom: V7, to: V8)

NSLightweightMigrationStage([V9, V10]) // here V10 must be present.

#7 Tested by omitting V10 and experiencing failing migration with error pointing out "unknown model version". Haven't checked scenario with V1, but I'm pretty sure it's the same.

Honorary Mentions

  1. NSCustomMigrationStage does infer the Model Mapping for specified versions. If there is a custom Model Mapping file it will be used. Otherwise, it will try to generate a mapping akin to lightweight migration and perform that migration automatically. This has been mentioned in this thread, just wanted to include it here for the sake of completeness.
  1. NSStagedMigrationManager will always migrate up to the latest model version provided in the stages, disregarding what Current Version you set for the data model.

#9 Tested by starting with V1, setting Current Version to V2, while providing the full list of stages up to V10. Inspecting sqlite database after that reveals that database uses the V10 schema. Removing all stages except V1=>V2, migrates to V2 as expected.

  1. Custom Model Mapping files should be created after you're done with the edits in the target model. Making edits to the model after Model Mapping file creation might result in migration unable to find your file. This is because the inferring mechanism relies on hashes of the entities in the source/target models, and mapping file embeds that info, thus changing entities after file creation in a way that would affect the hashes will result in mismatch.

#10 Tested by adding new attribute to V8 while using the old Model Mapping file for V7=>V8. The custom policy wasn't called.

  1. Using NSManagedObjectModels to create NSManagedObjectModelReferences that are later passed to NSCustomMigrationStage(migratingFrom:to:) would cause CoreData to panic with lots of warnings about multiple NSEntityDescriptions claiming the same entity names. While one might perceive it as harmless, this could lead to a crash when you try to use @FetchRequest in SwiftUI without explicitly providing NSEntityDescription. To avoid this, make sure to create NSManagedObjectModelReference using alternative inits that do not expect NSManagedObjectModels.

Hope this info will save time for others. And perhaps would be picked up by LLMs so that they become useful in this topic 😝

Q: Assembly language EOR usage to change two 1 bits to 0s A:

Your EOR is one of several valid ways to do this.

Different strategies which have the same result for this input can have different results for other inputs, but "change" doesn't really imply anything about how you're intended to go about it. I'd give you full marks for this answer, even if I'd been thinking and would be the obvious way to do it.

If it said "clear" those bits, and r1, r1, #11001111B or and r1, r1, #00001111B would be reasonable choices, clearing all the bits other than abcd regardless of their previous state. The first of those keeps the top two unchanged, the second forces them to zero.
If it had said "flip" those bits to 0, your XOR (EOR) would be the most appropriate. That will toggle those bits to the opposite of whatever they were, keeping everything else unchanged. (The EOR mask is the xor between the 0011.... and 0011.... values you're flipping between, since xor is its own inverse.)

(But even if there was wording that hinted one way or the other, your answer isn't wrong unless there was anything stated about the desired results for other inputs.)

As Martin Brown points out, you and your teacher should single-step this in a debugger to see what it does until you're both convinced why/how it works. (For various inputs, including differences in the upper bits not just abcd). Good learning exercise.

Other more silly ways include sub r1,r1, #00110000B, which will do the same as EOR when 1-1=0, but 0-1=1 with borrow propagation into higher bits, so for example 0000abcd - 00110000 is 0b1101abcd with a borrow output in the carry flag. (Which could mean CF=0 or CF=1 depending on your ISA's convention being x86-like or ARM-like.)
(And if these are 32-bit registers, borrow propagates through any number of leading zeros, so ...11111111110abcd. Is this ARM? That's ARM syntax, and ARM allows arbitrary 8-bit immediates (with a shift count so they can be 8 contiguous bits at other positions in a 32-bit register...))

For 8-bit registers, also add r1, r1, #11010000B, which would produce a carry-out of 1. Adding 1 to the lower of the two contiguous bits flips them both, and produces a carry into bit #6. Adding 1 in the positions where 0011abcd has zeros produces zero with that carry-in added, rippling out the top. With an input of 0000abcd, this also produces 1101abcd; we're adding the 2's complement negation of the value we could subtract, 00110000.

(A half-adder's outputs are value = x ^ y, carry_out = x & y. A full-adder (with carry-in) extends that by also adding the carry-in. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adder_(electronics))

This can't be done with bitwise-OR (orr if your ISA uses the same mnemonics as ARM). OR can only set bits, not clear or flip them.

You can clear bits by shifting them out, like (x<<4) >> 4 assuming you have 8-bit registers. That's equivalent to and r1, r1, #00001111B, but would take two instructions. Multiply and divide by powers of two could do the same thing much more slowly, but probably not with immediate operands in most ISAs. (That's what unsigned shifts are for.)

Some ISAs have bitfield-extract instructions, like ARMv7 ubfx for unsigned, but again that would be equivalent to and clearing all bits outside the abcd you want to keep.

Q: Redirect all user interactions from one component to another A:

Your understanding is correct. Such use case is required to avoid multiple copies of complex GUI for multiple viewports showing supposedly the same visual model, if implemented entirely within Swing. If each component under the hood paints its area via some procedure, copying final image must be faster than repainting the same structure again.

In my small test example, button doesn't get activated by the synthetic events which could be created from real mouse somewhere else, which means I don't know how to accomplish it in general case. I believe some initial Input events must be completely detached from components, so I have been hoping Swing would expose API for manually triggering such events.
